Open Mountain Status The local letter Weekly events and a local business spotlight, every Friday. Sign up at the bottom of this page What do you need a hand with? Start with your situation. These links take you to the people who handle it, with local help for food, housing, bills and everyday problems. Immediate danger or a medical emergency: call 911 . Don't use a website form to request emergency help. Need crisis support? Call 988 , text 988 , or chat with the 988 Lifeline , available around the clock. Get help Programs set their own requirements and availability. If you're unsure where to begin, call 211 or use 211 Santa Cruz County . I need groceries or help applying for benefits Mountain Community Resources in Felton offers food distribution and help with benefits applications. Call 831-335-6600 to ask what to bring and confirm the current schedule. I need shelter or help keeping my housing Start with 211's housing and shelter resources for current contacts and intake information. A listing doesn't guarantee a bed or financial assistance. For help navigating a housing problem, including an eviction concern, contact Mountain Community Resources . I'm having trouble paying an energy bill Central Coast Energy Services handles Home Energy Assistance Program applications for Santa Cruz County. Call 888-728-3637 to ask about applying. Assistance depends on program requirements and available funding. I need accessible transportation Lift Line has transportation programs for older adults and people with disabilities. Check the program that matches your trip, then ask about eligibility, service area, costs and booking before making plans. I'm helping an older adult or caring for someone Senior Network Services can help you find local support, care management and housing resources. Call 831-462-1433 and describe the help you or your family member needs. An older adult needs meals at home or nearby Meals on Wheels for Santa Cruz County offers home-delivered meals and community dining, including Highlands Park in Ben Lomond. Ask about screening, waitlists and the current dining schedule; home delivery isn't automatic. Who handles this? Boulder Creek has county roads, state highways and privately maintained roads. The right contact depends on the location. There's a problem on a county road For a county-maintained road, contact County Public Works . Road Operations dispatch is 831-477-3999 , available 24/7. Its contact page also links to the road-maintenance map and routine problem reports. Check maintenance responsibility first if you're on a private or association-maintained road. There's a problem on Highway 9 or 236 Use Caltrans' maintenance request form for a non-emergency state-highway issue. It isn't monitored for emergencies. Call 911 for a highway emergency. For current closures and incidents, check Caltrans QuickMap . The power is out Check or report an outage through PG&E's Outage Center . Follow PG&E's emergency guidance for electrical hazards. A missing outage marker doesn't establish that power is on or an area is safe. I have a water-service problem If SLVWD supplies your water, call 831-338-2153 . SLVWD's customer service page explains after-hours emergency calls. If you're served by a different water system, contact that provider. I need animal control or help with a stray Contact Santa Cruz County Animal Shelter : animal control 831-454-7224 , or after-hours animal emergencies 831-471-1182 . Use its current instructions for stray animals. I'm planning building, tree or property work Start with the county's Unified Permit Center to find the right permit team and ask about your parcel. Requirements depend on the work and location, so check before starting. Links and routing checked September 13, 2026. Confirm current service details with the provider. Suggest a correction . The details, when you need them. Open a topic for contacts, practical guidance and official links. Hours, fees, access and program availability can change. Check the linked provider before making plans. For home and everyday life Trash, recycling & pickup days GreenWaste picks up. The transfer station takes the rest. Boulder Creek is unincorporated Santa Cruz County, so collection runs through the county's franchise hauler. Curbside collection GreenWaste Recovery handles trash, recycling, and green waste for unincorporated Santa Cruz County. Customer service: 831-426-2711 . GreenWaste county page Your pickup day Enter your address in GreenWaste's lookup tool to see your collection day. That's also the fastest way to confirm your address is in their service area. Service day lookup Bulky items and extra pickups GreenWaste's county page lists up to three bulky item reuse collections and up to four extra set out collections per year at no additional charge. Call to schedule. Program details Self-haul: Ben Lomond Transfer Station 9835 Newell Creek Road, Ben Lomond, 831-454-2430 . Normal hours are Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, Friday and Saturday 7:30 am to 3:30 pm and Wednesday 7:30 am to 2:30 pm; closed Sunday. Construction runs to about September 2027, and while it lasts the open days vary with no day-by-day schedule posted, so check the improvement project page or call before hauling. The household hazardous waste facility is closed from August 21, 2026 through September 2027; use the alternatives listed on the project page. County solid waste page Water & power Two numbers worth saving in your phone. Both utilities take outage calls around the clock. Water: San Lorenzo Valley Water District If your home is served by the district, start or stop service through the Start and Stop Service page . Give at least 24 business hours of notice, and expect a $20 establishment fee on the first bill. Accounts go in the property owner's name. Customer service and emergencies: 831-338-2153 . After hours, the same number transfers to an answering service that reaches on-call staff, per the district's customer service page . Some properties in the area are on private wells or small mutual systems instead; your closing documents or neighbors can tell you which. Power: PG&E For a downed power line, stay away from it and anything it is touching, call 911, then call PG&E at 1-800-743-5000 . To report an outage, use the PG&E Outage Center or call 1-800-743-5002 . PG&E's general customer service line is 1-877-660-6789 . All three numbers are on PG&E's report an emergency page . Sign up for outage alerts so shutoffs don't catch you off guard. If someone in your home depends on power for qualifying medical needs, the Medical Baseline Program may provide an additional monthly energy allotment at a lower cost or a discount, depending on the rate plan, plus extra notifications ahead of Public Safety Power Shutoffs. Eligibility is based on medical need, not income. Internet & cell service Coverage varies canyon to canyon. These providers claim service in the Boulder Creek area on their own sites. Always check your exact address before signing anything; two houses on the same road can have different options. Xfinity (Comcast) Xfinity's local page states it provides internet service in the Boulder Creek area, with availability by address. Check your address AT&T AT&T's Boulder Creek page offers Internet Air fixed wireless, with fiber at some addresses. Availability is address by address. Check your address Starlink Satellite service that works independently of local lines, which matters during extended outages. Their site checks availability for a specific address. Check availability Cruzio The local Santa Cruz provider lists Boulder Creek in its service area, with an address lookup on its internet page. Check your address Ridge Wireless Fixed wireless internet that names Boulder Creek in its service area. Whether it reaches a house depends on the site, so it starts with a free site survey. Check coverage Cell coverage in the canyons is uneven for every carrier. Test your carrier at the house before you commit, and don't rely on cell alone for emergency alerts. A landline or satellite option is a reasonable backup here. Library, post office & recreation Library, post office, and rec programs. Three places that do a lot of quiet work in a small town. Boulder Creek Branch Library 13390 West Park Avenue. Part of Santa Cruz Public Libraries; hours and programs are on the branches page . Cards are free for California residents with photo ID and proof of address. Get a card Post office 200 Lorenzo Street, phone 831-338-4865 . Retail hours posted by USPS: Monday through Friday 9:30 am to 4:00 pm, closed weekends. Confirm current hours on the official page. USPS location page Recreation and parks The Boulder Creek Recreation and Park District runs local parks plus classes, camps, and community events, including adult classes and youth programs and classes . BCRPD site For family, property and local services Schools & families SLVUSD serves Boulder Creek. Enrollment starts with the school-site registrar, then online registration. The district's enrollment page lists age cutoffs and required documents. Boulder Creek Elementary TK through elementary grades at 400 Lomond Street, right in town. School site SLV Middle School The district middle school, located on the SLV campus in Felton. School site SLV High School The district high school, also in Felton on Highway 9. School site Preschools, child care, and referral services are listed in the local directory . Finding infant care up here is its own project; I wrote about how to do it, from experience . Permits, septic & tree work Check before you build, dig, or cut. Mountain parcels may involve septic, geologic, and tree requirements that vary by parcel. A short call to the county early can prevent delays and added cost. Building and zoning permits The county's Unified Permit Center, part of Community Development and Infrastructure , handles building, zoning, environmental, and public works permits for unincorporated areas like Boulder Creek. Permit Center Septic systems Most homes here are on septic. County Environmental Health runs the onsite wastewater program. A sewage disposal permit is required to install, upgrade, or abandon a system and for major and some minor repairs; routine maintenance may not require one. See the new-development rules and repair guidance . Septic rules Tree removal Some removals need a county permit, especially significant trees in the Coastal Zone and trees in sensitive habitat. Read the county's tree protection and removal page before scheduling work, and find local tree companies in the directory . Keep the practical details close, then make the day your own. Hours, fees, access and program availability can change. Check the linked provider before making plans. Getting here: roads and transit Plan the drive first. Boulder Creek sits on Highway 9. The roads in are winding and mostly two lanes, so give yourself extra time and check conditions before you leave. By car From Santa Cruz, take Highway 9 north up the valley through Felton and Ben Lomond. From the Santa Clara Valley side, Highway 9 climbs over the summit from Saratoga. A common alternative from Highway 17 is Bear Creek Road, which drops into Boulder Creek from the east. All three are slow mountain roads with tight curves, cyclists, and wildlife, so use pullouts to let faster traffic by. Check the roads Winter storms and summer roadwork both close lanes up here. Check Caltrans QuickMap for real-time closures and chain controls, and the County Road Closure Dashboard for local roads. Our Mountain Status page pulls together the same sources. Cell service is patchy along parts of Highway 9, so it helps to have directions saved before you lose signal. Riding the bus? Santa Cruz METRO usually connects Boulder Creek and the San Lorenzo Valley with Santa Cruz through Route 35 and the weekday express Route 35X . Route 35 covers nights and weekends. Holiday schedules and service changes can affect trips, so check METRO before you leave. Parks, access and local recreation Parks and trails nearby. Big Basin access keeps changing as recovery from the 2020 CZU fire continues. Confirm hours, reservations, and open trails on each park's official page the day you go. Big Basin Redwoods State Park California's oldest state park is open for limited day use as it recovers from the CZU fire, and much of it remains closed. Parking is limited; reservations are encouraged but not required. Day-use parking is $6 with a $2 reservation fee or $10 without a reservation. There is no fee to arrive by foot, bike, or bus. Potable water is not available, although bottled water is sold at the kiosk. Confirm current access before you drive up. Big Basin access, State Parks Castle Rock State Park Sandstone formations and ridge-top views along Skyline. The park is on Highway 35 about two and a half miles southeast of the Highway 9 junction. Parking is $10 per vehicle, and the park is open from 6 am to sunset. Weekdays are usually quieter for parking. Castle Rock, State Parks Fall Creek, Henry Cowell A quiet day-use unit with about twenty miles of trails through redwoods and old lime kilns. The trailhead and free parking are on Felton Empire Road off Highway 9. There are no facilities, and dogs, bikes, and fires are not allowed. Henry Cowell, State Parks Closer to town, the Boulder Creek Recreation and Park District keeps up Junction Park , with a small beach, San Lorenzo River access, a lawn, and picnic tables one block off the main street. Barbara Day Park sits just downstream, and Garrahan Park up Highway 9 has a walking track, fields, and barbecue areas. The river beach at Junction Park is where Boulder Creek kids learn to swim, mine included, and it runs on the same arrangement it always has: little kids on the sand, bigger kids on the rocks, cold water for everyone. It's swim at your own risk. The fuller day: places and options A perfect day in Boulder Creek. Five stops, with room to make the day yours. This is the itinerary I give friends when they visit. Hours change up here, so check before you count on any single stop. Start with breakfast Jenna Sue's Coffee and a casual downtown start. The Tree House Cafe The other local coffee stop, made for lingering. Bella's Cafe The town's sit-down breakfast. Earn your lunch Play a round Nine holes under the redwoods at the Boulder Creek Golf and Country Club . Swim The rec district pool in season, or the river beach at Junction Park. Hike Big Basin Limited day-use as the park recovers; check access first . Stop for lunch Taqueria Los Gallos Burritos and tacos, no ceremony. El Rey Leon Mexican food truck on the main drag. Walk the shops The main stretch rewards a slow lap: Air and Fire for crystals and gifts, SWAG's eclectic collective, Viscosity Glass for locally made glass art, Beck's Shoes, fitting families since 1919, and Scarborough's hardware and garden aisles with a little of everything. The directory has the full list with hours. Stay for dinner Tae's Edo Sushi Bar Sushi and Japanese dinner plates. Scopazzi's Historic Italian dining room and lounge. Red Pearl Chinese, dine-in or takeout. Stay the night Make it a weekend. Our guide to where to stay in Boulder Creek covers the lodging from downtown out toward Big Basin, and the directory lists each place with its contact details. Full details, hours, and phone numbers for every spot are on Food and Drink . What to know through the seasons What the seasons ask of you. Conditions shape a visit more than the calendar does. Check before you come. Winter Storms bring downed trees, flooding, and road closures on Highway 9 and the back roads. Check Mountain Status and Caltrans QuickMap before heading up, and turn around if a road looks unsafe. Summer The valley can be warm and the river draws crowds. Bring water, watch your footing on rocks, keep an eye on kids near moving water, and pack out everything you bring. Fire season This is a fire-prone forest. No fires or charcoal outside designated areas, and never during a Red Flag Warning. Check fire weather with the National Weather Service and CAL FIRE before you go. Practical details and visiting like a neighbor The practical stuff. There's one gas station in town on Highway 9, so fill up before long drives or a trip out to Big Basin. Groceries and markets are on the food and drink page. Public restrooms are limited, so plan around them. Remember that cell service drops out along stretches of Highway 9. Visit like a neighbor. Most of what looks like open forest is someone's home, watershed, or working land. Leave no trace and pack out your trash. Don't park on blind curves or block driveways and pullouts. Keep noise down near houses, follow all fire restrictions, and give the road and the river the caution they're due. Leave room for a local story. How to read this page What each panel checks, and who publishes it What these panels will not tell you When a panel says unavailable Questions we get Related pages on Boulder Creek Local Official information National Weather Service CruzAware Caltrans QuickMap Santa Cruz County road closures PG&E outage map AirNow Fire and Smoke Map CAL FIRE incidents See something that needs attention? Boulder Creek Mountain Status: Weather, Roads and Outages 0 Conditions and official links Mountain Status A quick starting point for weather, smoke, roads, outages, and emergency information affecting Boulder Creek. This is not an emergency alert service. For immediate danger, call 911. Confirm urgent information with the responsible agency. Live conditions Current mountain snapshot Live status is available below. The forecast, NWS alerts, a modeled air-quality estimate and official source links load fresh inside the tool each time you open the page. Loading live conditions. If they do not appear, use the official sources below. How to read this page Every panel in the snapshot above is fetched from the agency that publishes it at the moment you open this page. Nothing is written ahead of time, nothing is cached overnight, and nothing here decides whether a road, a river, or the air is fine. Those calls belong to the agencies below, and in an emergency they belong to 911. Boulder Creek Local is a community guide, not an alert service. What this page does is put the official screens in one place and say plainly where each number came from, so you can reach the source in one click when it matters. What follows does not change from day to day: it is the map of the page, not a report on conditions. What each panel checks, and who publishes it Air quality. A modeled US AQI and PM2.5 estimate for downtown Boulder Creek from Open-Meteo . A model is not a monitor. During a smoke event the ground monitors on the AirNow Fire and Smoke Map are the ones to work from, and in a canyon they can differ from a modeled figure by a wide margin. Highway closures. The Caltrans District 5 lane closure feed, filtered to Santa Cruz County on Highways 1, 9, 17, 35, and 236. State highways only. County-maintained roads, including Bear Creek Road, Jamison Creek Road, and China Grade, are not in that feed at all. For those, use the Santa Cruz County road dashboard , and check Caltrans QuickMap for the state routes before you drive. San Lorenzo River. Gage height in feet and streamflow in cubic feet per second from USGS gauge 11160500, San Lorenzo River at Big Trees, in Felton. It is the nearest real-time gauge downstream of Boulder Creek, so it reads the valley rather than the town. The panel prints the reading, the time it was taken, and the National Weather Service stages published for forecast point BTEC1, and it stops there. Turning a reading into a flood call is the NWS river forecast 's job, not ours. Weather forecast and alerts. The National Weather Service API, queried for a single point, downtown Boulder Creek. Alerts are point specific: a warning in force over another part of Santa Cruz County may not appear here at all. The full county picture is at the NWS Bay Area office . Power. Direct links to the PG&E outage map, the outage alert signup for your address, and the report line. Boulder Creek Local does not read a PG&E feed and does not restate one. The outage map is the source. Sirens and smoke. Links to the same screens dispatchers feed. PulsePoint shows Boulder Creek Fire Protection District calls with the units responding. Watch Duty carries human-verified wildfire updates. The CAL FIRE incident list covers state incidents. The ALERTCalifornia cameras at Brookdale and Mt. Bielawski are steerable cameras for situational awareness. The CHP dispatch log lists highway incidents under the Monterey Communications Center, which covers Highways 9 and 236. The Sheriff's calls-for-service lookup is a records search by address, not a live feed. What these panels will not tell you Whether anything is safe. No panel converts a reading into advice. A number is published with its source and its timestamp, and the judgment stays with the agency that owns it. What is not being shown. An empty feed means not shown, not nothing happening. Law enforcement calls are generally not published live anywhere public, and several incident types are excluded from the Sheriff's lookup by policy. Evacuation information. Zones, warnings, and orders come from CruzAware and from the agency issuing them. That is the one thing this page will never summarize, paraphrase, or delay. A reading you can rely on later. Each panel is read once, when the page loads, and the timestamp on the snapshot says so. Reload to read it again. If what you see here disagrees with an agency's own page, the agency is right. Final numbers. USGS river data arrives provisional and is revised afterward. The panel labels it that way for a reason. When a panel says unavailable Unavailable means the feed did not answer, or answered with something the page could not read. It never means the condition is fine. Missing data is missing, and the useful response is to go straight to the source. Air quality unavailable: AirNow Fire and Smoke Map . Roads unavailable: Caltrans QuickMap for state highways, the county road dashboard for county roads. River unavailable: the USGS gauge page and the NWS river forecast . Weather unavailable: the NWS Bay Area office and its Boulder Creek point forecast. Anything involving fire or smoke: Watch Duty and the CAL FIRE incident list , with CruzAware for anything that becomes an order. Three numbers worth keeping in your phone. Report a power outage to PG&E at 1-800-743-5002 . For a downed power line, call 911 first, then PG&E at 1-800-743-5000 . For a tree or a slide on a county-maintained road, Santa Cruz County road dispatch is 831-477-3999 . Questions we get Is this an official alert service? No. Boulder Creek Local is an independent community guide with no dispatch role and no standing with any agency. Official alerts for Santa Cruz County come through CruzAware , which takes a few minutes to sign up for and is the most useful link on this page. Emergencies go to 911. Why does the page not just say whether Highway 9 is passable? Because the feed cannot hold that sentence up. Caltrans publishes lane closures on its own schedule, so a closure that started minutes ago may not be in the data yet, and a county road closure will never be in it. A page that printed an all clear would be guessing, and guessing about a mountain road is how somebody ends up driving into one. My road is not a state highway. Where do I look? The county road dashboard covers county-maintained roads, and Santa Cruz County road dispatch takes reports at 831-477-3999 . Private roads and shared driveways belong to their owners or road associations, which is worth knowing before a storm rather than during one. The air quality figure here does not match the app on my phone. Which is right? They measure different things. The panel above is a model, an estimate built from regional conditions for a point in Boulder Creek. Most phone apps blend monitors, and smoke apps read sensors directly. When smoke is the question, use the ground monitors on the AirNow Fire and Smoke Map and treat the modeled number as background context. What is gage height, and is a given reading high? Gage height is the height of the water surface above the gauge's own reference point. It is not the depth of the river and it is not comparable between gauges. Streamflow, in cubic feet per second, is the volume moving past the gauge. Whether a reading matters is answered by the National Weather Service stages for that gauge, published on the NWS river forecast page . The panel quotes those stages with attribution and does not invent its own. I heard sirens. How do I find out what that was? Start with PulsePoint for fire and medical calls in the Boulder Creek Fire Protection District, then the CHP dispatch log for highway collisions and Watch Duty for anything that looks like wildfire. Law enforcement calls are generally not visible in real time, so a screen with nothing on it is not an answer to what you heard. How often does this page update? Every time you load it. There is no overnight refresh and no stored copy of a previous reading. That is also why the snapshot carries the time it was retrieved: it is telling you how old the data on your screen already is. Can Boulder Creek Local text me when something happens? No, and we would not want to sit between you and an evacuation order. Sign up with CruzAware for county alerts, PG&E outage alerts for your address, and the PulsePoint Respond and Watch Duty apps for calls and wildfire. Those come from the agencies themselves, with no extra link in the chain. records.s: Finding a long-term rental in Boulder Creek and the San Lorenzo Valley: current verified listings and what to know before you sign.
records.k: The local letter Useful local information, gathered with care. Rentals in Boulder Creek and the San Lorenzo Valley 0 Places to live Rentals in the San Lorenzo Valley This is a small board, and it usually will be. The valley has very little rental stock, a good share of it changes hands privately, and what does get listed tends to go quickly. A short list here isn't a sign the board is broken. It's an accurate picture of a thin market. Listings cover long-term rentals in Boulder Creek, Ben Lomond, Brookdale and Felton, drawn from property managers and public listings. Each one shows when it was last confirmed, so you can tell a fresh listing from a stale one, and each links back to its original source. The board refreshes each morning, and the date it last ran is shown at the top. Before you send anyone money Never wire money, send a deposit, or pay an application fee before you've seen the place in person and confirmed who you're dealing with. Rental scams follow tight markets, and this is one. A listing that pressures you to pay quickly, or asks you to pay before viewing, is a listing to walk away from. Boulder Creek Local isn't the landlord, the property manager, or a party to any agreement. We publish what's listed publicly, and we can be wrong. The rest of the market Because so much of the valley's renting happens outside listing sites, people who find places here usually do it by being visible locally: the community boards on Facebook, a note at the market, telling neighbors you're looking. Most valley rentals are filled before they're ever advertised, and that matches what turns up on this board. If you're new to the area, Resident Resources covers what to sort out once you land: water, power, trash, internet, and what living on a septic system and a mountain road actually involves. records.s: Season rainfall totals for Boulder Creek and the San Lorenzo Valley, tracked against the water year using NOAA records from Ben Lomond since 1937.
records.k: What this measures How missing data is handled The record, in short The local letter Useful local information, gathered with care. Boulder Creek Rainfall: San Lorenzo Valley Rain Tracker 0 San Lorenzo Valley rain tracker How much rain has the valley actually had? Season-to-date rainfall at the valley's longest gauge, with records dating to 1937. Water year totals, storm totals, and the wettest and driest years on record. The historical summary below was checked October 20, 2026. This is a record, not a warning. For roads, air quality, the river gauge and official alerts, use Mountain Status . In an emergency, call 911. What this measures Rainfall on this page comes from one National Weather Service cooperative gauge: Ben Lomond No. 4 , station USC00040673, at 435 feet, about five miles down-canyon from downtown Boulder Creek. It has logged daily rainfall since 1937 and is still reporting. It is used here because it is the only gauge near the valley with a record long enough to say what normal means. Readings are read through the NOAA Regional Climate Centers ACIS service. Totals are counted by water year , October 1 through September 30, named for the calendar year it ends in. A water year holds exactly one winter, which is how storms actually arrive. Splitting rainfall by calendar year cuts every wet season in half and makes two winters impossible to compare. Ben Lomond No. 4 is a once-a-day gauge and its readings reach NOAA on a delay, so the last day or two of a storm often has not arrived yet. That is why every figure on this page wears the date it was read. It is a history layer, not a live feed. How missing data is handled Some days in this record have no reading at all. Those gaps are counted, published, and left alone. Nothing is estimated, interpolated, or filled in from a neighbouring gauge. A water year missing more than five days is excluded from every average, percentile band and ranking on this page. In the snapshot checked October 20, 2026, 68 water years are complete enough to report , covering 1940 through 2026. The excluded years are named rather than hidden. The largest gaps fall in 1937 through 1939, 1941, 2011, 2012 and 2024. Water year 2025 is missing fourteen days plus one multi-day accumulated total, so it is reported as approximate and left out of the averages. A season total that contains a gap is described as a floor , not a total: the real figure is that much or more. The tool says how many readings are missing and on which dates, because a missed day in January can cost inches while a missed day in July costs almost nothing. A trace, less than five thousandths of an inch, is a real observation and counts as zero. A missing day is not zero and is never treated as a dry day. If the gauge stops reporting, the page says the record is behind. A season total that has stopped moving means the readings have stopped arriving, not that it has stopped raining. Daily water-year totals are compared with the monthly aggregation where both series exist. A disagreement prevents publication. Years without a monthly comparison are identified in the interactive methodology. The record, in short Across the 68 reportable water years in that snapshot, the average is 49.03 inches and the median is 42.72 inches . A handful of enormous years pull the average above the middle of the record. The seasonal median describes the middle of this water-year record; it does not size a culvert, ditch or storage tank. Drainage design needs site-specific peak design flow and design-storm analysis. Ask a qualified local engineer and the permitting agency about your site. The wettest water years on record are 1983 at 95.65 inches, 2017 at 94.62, 2023 at 85.13, 1998 at 82.80 and 1958 at 80.61. The driest are 1977 at 19.97 inches, 2021 at 21.51, 1976 at 21.60, 2014 at 22.83 and 1990 at 24.30. The wettest single day in the whole record is January 4, 1982, at 11.47 inches. Water year 2021 and water year 2023 sit two years apart: 21.51 inches and 85.13 inches. A four-fold swing inside two winters is not an anomaly here, it is the shape of the record, and it is the reason the word average does so little work in this valley. One gauge is not a valley. Rainfall at your own place will differ with elevation, canyon and aspect. The full write-up of this record covers how closely Boulder Creek tracks Ben Lomond, and what the swings mean for a house up here. records.s: Learn why Boulder Creek Local is building a practical, source-aware community guide for residents, neighbors, and visitors.
records.k: It started with a childcare search. Why Boulder Creek Local? Born here. Still here. Helping our community connect. A free community resource. The local letter Useful local information, gathered with care. About Boulder Creek Local 0 About the project A local connection. A useful place to start. A community resource for finding what you need, discovering what's happening, and getting to know Boulder Creek. Why this exists It started with a childcare search. When our baby arrived and my return to work started counting down, I went looking for infant care and found almost nothing to look at. The valley's providers are real, and some are wonderful, but most have no website and no active social media, so as far as the internet is concerned they barely exist. I found our spot the old mountain way: through word of mouth, one recommendation at a time, while the clock ran. Somewhere in those conversations it clicked that this valley solves most of its problems the same way, and that somebody should start writing the answers down. This site is me writing the answers down. The name Why Boulder Creek Local? The name comes from how I've always described myself: a Boulder Creek local, born and raised. I grew up here, and now I'm raising my own family here. This website grew out of that connection and a desire to make useful local information easier to find and share. Who's behind it Born here. Still here. I'm Adrienne. I was born and raised in Boulder Creek and never really left: my partner and I are raising our family here on a small homestead with chickens, ducks, one opinionated goose named Lucy, dogs, cats, and a garden that wins some years and loses others. I've swum in the river at Junction Park since before I could ride a bike, and these days I get to watch the next generation discover the same sandy beach. I believe in shopping local and in the businesses that keep a small town running, and I believe information about this town should be as easy to find as the town is easy to love. Our goal Helping our community connect. The goal is to make everyday life a little easier for locals. That means bringing useful information together, helping people find local services, and making it easier to discover businesses, events, and opportunities to get involved. I also want to help the people doing good work here be easier to find. Many local businesses and community groups rely on word of mouth. Boulder Creek Local gives neighbors another way to discover them, support them, and share what they find. For the community A free community resource. Boulder Creek Local is free to use. No one pays to be listed in the directory or featured in our editorial coverage, and we don't run advertising. Listings and articles help readers learn what's available. Inclusion isn't an endorsement, and details can change. Updates, corrections, and suggestions are always welcome.
